title: Scattering amplitudes from quantum hardware a la RESOs
authors: Raul A Briceno, Ivan M Burbano, Anthony N Ciavarella, Ermal Rrapaj, Thomas R Richardson, Andre Walker-Loud
abstract: We report the first quantum-hardware implementation of Real-time Estimators for Scattering Observables (RESOs). The physical model is a one-dimensional lattice theory of non-relativistic spin-1/2 fermions with a single contact interaction. The lattice sizes studied are up to $N_x=54$ lattice sites and up to $20$ time steps. Spacetime correlation functions were computed on IBM's quantum computers, using $109$ qubits with $10,806$ CZ gates applied, reaching a two-qubit gate depth of $246$. We demonstrate how to study bound states and extract scattering amplitudes from these correlation functions.
summary: This work pioneers the use of quantum hardware to calculate scattering amplitudes for a simple lattice fermion model using the RESOs protocol. By measuring real-time correlation functions on an IBM quantum computer, the authors successfully extract scattering phase shifts, validating the method against classical simulations. This represents a significant step toward simulating complex quantum field theories on quantum processors.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of calculating fundamental scattering amplitudes in quantum field theories using near-term quantum hardware.
main_result: The authors report the first successful quantum-hardware implementation of the Real-time Estimators for Scattering Observables (RESOs) method for a 1D lattice fermion model.
method: They compute finite-volume real-time correlators on an IBM quantum processor, projecting these measurements to extract energy-dependent scattering phase shifts.
model_or_system: The physical model is a one-dimensional lattice theory of non-relativistic spin-1/2 fermions with a contact interaction, described by a lattice Hamiltonian derived from a continuum Lagrangian.
key_observables: Scattering amplitudes, scattering phase shifts ($\cot \delta / \sin(a p^*)$), and real-time correlation functions $C(t, x)$.
important_parameters: Lattice size up to $N_x=54$ sites, up to 20 time steps, and a benchmark bound state energy $E^\star_B = -9.4 	ext{ MeV}$ for $g=-0.2$.
main_assumptions: The method relies on mapping fermions to qubits via Jordan-Wigner transformation and uses specific error mitigation techniques to extract energy information.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares the estimator error against analytical and tensor network results; Figure 2 illustrates the path from circuit measurements to energy-dependent correlation functions.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the RESOs method for scattering observables, details the implementation on quantum hardware for the 1D fermion model, presents results showing consistency with classical benchmarks, and discusses future scalability.
why_interesting: It demonstrates a concrete, advanced application of quantum computation (RESOs) to a core problem in particle/nuclear physics (scattering amplitudes), bridging quantum information science with high-energy theory.

FIG. 2. Shown are the three main stages of the correlation functions obtained from the quantum hardware. The top left panel shows the correlation functions in space and time for Nx = 54 spatial lattices. The white line shows the light cone of the quantum circuit used to simulate time evolution. The top right panel shows the result after Fourier transforming to definite spatial momentum for two momenta. The bottom right panel shows the correlator after Fourier transforming to energy for a fixed total atϵ = 1. The dashed line labels the location of the negative binding energy of the “deuteron” bound state. The bottom left panel shows the scattering phase shifts computed from these correlators.
